definition: The CIA triad is a common model that forms the basis for the development of security systems. They are used for finding vulnerabilities and methods for creating solutions.

term: National Institute of Standards and Technology
definition: Develops computer security standards used by US federal agencies and publishes cybersecurity best practice guides and research.
Standards, best practices, and guidelines for effective security risk management. Some frameworks are general in nature, while others are specific to industry or technology types.
A technology or procedure put in place to mitigate vulnerabilities and risk and to ensure the confidentiality, integrity, and availability (CIA) of information.
An analysis that measures the difference between the current and desired states in order to help assess the scope of work included in a project.

A security process that provides identification, authentication, and authorization mechanisms for users, computers, and other entities to work with organizational assets like networks, operating systems, and applications.
Tracking authorized usage of a resource or use of rights by a subject and alerting when unauthorized use is detected or attempted.
A security concept where a centralized platform verifies subject identification, ensures the subject is assigned relevant permissions, and then logs these actions to create an audit trail.
Relies on a person for implementation
Devices that mediate access to premises and hardware
Acts before an incident to eliminate or reduce the likelihood that an attack can succeed.

The collection of access control entries (ACEs) that determines which subjects (user accounts, host IP addresses, and so on) are allowed or denied access to the object and the privileges given (read-only, read/write, and so on).
acts during an incident to identify or record that it is happening.
Acts after an incident to eliminate or minimize its impact.
Enforces a rule of behavior through a policy or contract.
Discourages intrusion attempts.
Takes on risk mitigation when a primary control fails or cannot completely meet expectations.
A company officer with the primary responsibility for management of information technology assets and procedures.
Typically the job title of the person with overall responsibility for information assurance and systems security.
Organizational role with technical responsibilities for implementation of security policies, frameworks, and controls.
The location where security professionals monitor and protect critical information assets in an organization.
A combination of software development and systems operations, and refers to the practice of integrating one discipline with the other.
A combination of software development, security operations, and systems operations, and refers to the practice of integrating each discipline with the others.
Team with responsibility for incident response.
Likelihood and impact (or consequence) of a threat actor exercising a vulnerability.
The ability of threat actors to draw upon funding to acquire personnel, tools, and to develop novel attack types.
A type of attack that compromises the availability of an asset or business process.
Demanding payment to prevent the release of information.
Often used to refer to someone who breaks into computer systems or spreads viruses, ethical hackers prefer to think of themselves as experts on and explorers of computer security systems.
A hacker engaged in authorized penetration testing or other security consultancy.
An inexperienced, unskilled attacker that typically uses tools or scripts created by others.
A type of threat actor that is supported by the resources of its host country's military and security services.
A threat actor that causes a vulnerability or exposes an attack vector without malicious intent.
The path that a threat actor uses to execute a data exfiltration, service disruption, or disinformation attack.
Weakness that could be triggered accidentally or exploited intentionally to cause a security breach.
Product life cycle phase where mainstream vendor support is no longer available.
Configuration that exposes a large attack surface, such as through unnecessary open service ports, weak or no authentication, use of default credentials, or lack of secure communications/encryption.
Will entice a victim into using or opening a removable device, document, image, or program that conceals malware.
The end-to-end process of supplying, manufacturing, distributing, and finally releasing goods and services to a customer.
Using persuasion, manipulation, or intimidation to make the victim violate a security policy.
Social engineering attack where an attacker pretends to be someone they are not.
Social engineering tactic where a team will communicate, whether directly or indirectly, a lie or half-truth in order to get someone to believe a falsehood.
A type of email-based social engineering attack, in which the attacker sends email from a supposedly reputable source, such as a bank, to try to elicit private information from the victim.
A human-based attack where the attacker extracts information while speaking over the phone or leveraging IP-based voice messaging services (VoIP).
A form of phishing that uses SMS text messages to trick a victim into revealing information.
An impersonation attack in which a request for a website, typically an e-commerce site, is redirected to a similar-looking, but fake, website.

An attack in which an attacker registers a domain name with a common misspelling of an existing domain, so that a user who misspells a URL they enter into a browser is taken to the attacker's website.
An impersonation attack in which the attacker gains control of an employee's account and uses it to convince other employees to perform fraudulent actions.
An attack in which an attacker targets specific groups or organizations, discovers which websites they frequent, and injects malicious code into those sites.
The science and practice of altering data to make it unintelligible to unauthorized parties.
The art of cracking cryptographic systems.
Scrambling the characters used in a message so that the message can be seen but not understood or modified unless it can be deciphered.
A specific piece of information that is used in conjunction with an algorithm to perform encryption and decryption.
Two-way encryption scheme in which encryption and decryption are both performed by the same key. Also known as shared-key encryption.
Size of a cryptographic key in bits.
Cipher that uses public and private keys.
A function that converts an arbitrary-length string input to a fixed-length string output.
A cryptographic hashing algorithm created to address possible weaknesses in MDA.
A framework of certificate authorities, digital certificates, software, services, and other cryptographic components deployed for the purpose of validating subject identities.
In PKI, a public CA that issues certificates for multiple domains and is widely trusted as a root trust by operating systems and browsers.

Identification and authentication information presented in the X.509 format and issued by a certificate authority (CA) as a guarantee that a key pair (as identified by the public key embedded in the certificate) is valid for a particular subject (user or host).
A set of standards to promote the use of public key infrastructure.
In PKI, a CA that issues certificates to intermediate CAs in a hierarchical structure.
A method of validating a certificate by tracing each CA that signs the certificate, up through the hierarchy to the root CA. Also referred to as chain of trust.
A digital certificate that has been signed by the entity that issued it, rather than by a CA.
A Base64 ASCII file that a subject sends to a CA to get a certificate.
In PKI, a digital certificate that will match multiple subdomains of a parent domain.
A list of certificates that were revoked before their expiration date.
In PKI, procedures and tools that centralizes generation and storage of cryptographic keys.
A measure of disorder. Cryptographic systems should exhibit high entropy to better resist brute force attacks.
Specification for secure hardware-based storage of encryption keys, hashed passwords, and other user- and platform-identification information.
An appliance for generating and storing cryptographic keys.
Methods exposed by a script or program that allow other scripts or programs to use it.
CPU extensions that protect data stored in system memory so that an untrusted process cannot read it.
The storage of a backup key with a third party.
Information that is primarily stored on specific media, rather than moving from one medium to another.

term: Data in transit (or data in motion)
definition: Information that is being transmitted between two hosts, such as over a private network or the Internet.

term: Data in use (or data in processing)
definition: Information that is present in the volatile memory of a host, such as system memory or cache.
Encryption scheme applied to data-in-motion, such as WPA, IPsec, or TLS.
Any method by which cryptographic keys are transferred among users.
A method used to verify both the integrity and authenticity of a message by combining a cryptographic hash of the message with a secret key.
A characteristic of transport encryption that ensures if a key is compromised, the compromise will only affect a single session and not facilitate recovery of plaintext data from other sessions.
A cryptographic technique that provides secure key exchange.
A security countermeasure that mitigates the impact of precomputed hash table attacks by adding a random value to ("salting") each plaintext input.
A concept in which an expanding list of transactional records listed in a public ledger is secured using cryptography.
Distributed public record of transactions that underpins the integrity of blockchains.
A technique that essentially "hides" or "camouflages" code or other information so that it is harder to read by unauthorized users.
Hiding a message in a picture or file.
something you know/have/are for implementing authentication
Rules to govern secure selection and maintenance of knowledge factor authentication secrets.
A set of rules governing user security information, which can be set globally.
An authentication scheme that requires the user to present at least two different factors as credentials.
A biometric assessment metric that measures the number of unauthorized users who are mistakenly allowed access.
A security device similar to a credit card that can store authentication information on an embedded cryptoprocessor.
A password that is generated for use in one specific session and becomes invalid after the session ends.
OTP sent to a registered number or email account or generated by an authenticator app as a means of two-step verification when authenticating account access.
Capability of an authenticator or other cryptographic module to prove that it is a root of trust and can provide reliable reporting to prove that a device or computer is a trustworthy platform.
Security settings that control access to objects including file system items and network resources.
An access control model where each resource is protected by an access control list (ACL) managed by the resource's owner (or owners).
An access control model where resources are protected by inflexible, system-defined rules.
An access control model where resources are protected by ACLs that are managed by administrators and that provide user permissions based on job functions.
a collection of user accounts with the same level of access.
An access control technique that evaluates a set of attributes that each subject possesses to determine if access should be granted.
A nondiscretionary access control technique that is based on a set of operational rules or restrictions to enforce a least privileges permissions policy.
A basic principle of security stating that something should be allocated the minimum necessary rights, privileges, or information to perform its role.
The value assigned to an account by Windows and that is used by the operating system to identify that account.
On a Windows domain, a way to deploy per-user and per-computer settings.
The identification or estimation of the physical location of an object.
aka: radar source, mobile phone, or Internet-connected computing device.

definition: Policies or configuration settings that limit a user's access to resources.
Policies, procedures, and support software for managing accounts and credentials with administrative permissions.
A challenge-response authentication protocol created by Microsoft for use in its products.
A framework for implementing authentication providers in Linux.
A network service that stores identity information about all the objects in a particular network.
aka: users, groups, servers, client computers, printers

definition: Protocol used to access network directory databases
Authentication technology that enables a user to authenticate once and receive authorizations for multiple services.
A single sign-on authentication and authorization service that is based on a time-sensitive, ticket-granting system.
In Kerberos, a token issued to an authenticated account to allow access to authorized application servers.
A process that provides a shared login capability across multiple systems and enterprises.
An XML-based data format used to exchange authentication information between a client and a service.
A standardized, stateless architectural style used by web applications for communication and integration.
A standard for federated identity management, allowing resource servers or consumer sites to work with user accounts created and managed on a separate identity provider.
A private network facility that is owned and operated by an organization for use by its employees only.
any broadcast domain that is partitioned and isolated in a computer network at the data link layer (OSI layer 2).
The points at which a network or application receive external connections or inputs/outputs that are potential vectors to be exploited by a threat actor.
Preventing a device attached to a switch port from communicating on the network unless it matches a given MAC address or other protection profile.
Applying an access control list to a switch or access point so that only clients with approved MAC addresses can connect to it.
A standard for encapsulating EAP communications over a LAN (EAPoL) or WLAN (EAPoW) to implement port-based authentication.
In EAP architecture, the device requesting access to the network.
Framework for negotiating authentication methods that enable systems to use hardware-based identifiers.
AAA protocol used to manage remote and wireless authentication infrastructures.
The process of choosing the type and placement of security controls to ensure the goals of the CIA triad and compliance with any framework requirements.
An enumeration, vulnerability, or incident detection scan that analyzes only intercepted network traffic rather than sending probes to a target.
Detective and preventive security controls that use an agent or network configuration to monitor hosts.
Placement and configuration of a network security control so that it becomes part of the cable path.
A hardware device inserted into a cable run to copy frames for analysis.
A Layer 3 firewall technology that compares packet headers against ACLs to determine which network traffic to accept.
A standalone hardware device that performs only the function of a firewall, which is embedded into the appliance's firmware.
A hardware device that has the primary function of a router, but also has firewall functionality embedded into the router firmware.
A stateful inspection firewall that can monitor TCP sessions and UDP traffic.
A stateful inspection firewall that can filter traffic based on specific application protocol headers and data.
A server that mediates the communications between a client and another server.
A feature of many proxy servers that enables the servers to retain a copy of frequently requested web pages.
A server that redirects requests and responses for clients configured with the proxy address and port.
A server that redirects requests and responses without the client being explicitly configured to use it.
A type of proxy server that protects servers from direct contact with client requests.

An open source NIDS. A subscription ("oinkcode") is required to obtain up-to-date rulesets, which allow the detection engine to identify the very latest threats. Non-subscribers can obtain community-authored rulesets.
Advances in firewall technology
A type of switch, router, or software that distributes client requests between different resources.
A scheduling approach used by load balancers to route traffic to devices that have already established connections with the client in question.
the configuration option that enables a client to maintain a connection with a load-balanced server over the duration of the session. Also referred to as sticky sessions.
A firewall designed specifically to protect software running on web servers and their back-end databases from code injection and DoS attacks.
A secure tunnel created between two endpoints connected via an unsecure transport network (typically the Internet).
The practice of encapsulating data from one protocol for safe transfer over another network such as the Internet.
Virtual private networking solution that uses digital certificates to identify and host and establish secure tunnels for network traffic.
Virtual private networking (VPN).
IPSec protocol that provides authentication for the origin of transmitted data as well as integrity and protection against replay attacks.
IPSec sub-protocol that enables encryption and authentication of the header and payload of a data packet.
Framework for creating a security association (SA) used with IPSec.
Remote access tool and protocol. VNC is the basis of macOS screen sharing.
Using features of HTML5 to implement remote desktop/VPN connections via browser software (clientless).
Accessing the administrative interface of a network appliance using a separate network from the usual data network.
A hardened server that provides access to other hosts.
Classifying the ownership and management of a cloud as public, private, community, or hybrid.
A cloud that is deployed for shared use by multiple independent tenants.
Organization providing infrastructure, application, and/or storage services via an "as a service" subscription-based, cloud-centric offering.
A cloud deployment model where the cloud consumer uses mutiple public cloud services.
A cloud that is deployed for use by a single entity.
Computing architecture where on-demand resources provisioned with the attributes of high availability, scalability, and elasticity are billed to customers on the basis of metered utilization.
A cloud deployment that uses both private and public elements.
Classifying the provision of cloud services and the limit of the cloud service provider's responsibility as software, platform, infrastructure, etc
A cloud service model that provisions application and database services as a platform for development of apps.
A cloud service model that provisions virtual machines and network infrastructure.

Identifies that responsibility for the implementation of security as applications, data, and workloads are transitioned into a cloud platform are shared between the customer and the cloud service provider (CSP).
A model where all data processing and storage is performed in a single location.
A model in which data processing and storage are distributed across multiple locations or devices.
A metric that defines how closely systems approach the goal of providing data availability 100% of the time while maintaining a high level of system performance.
A software delivery model where the code runs on a server and is streamed to a client.
offloads infrastructure management to the cloud service provider
aka: configuring file storage capability without the requirement of first building and deploying a file server.

definition: A private network segment made available to a single cloud consumer on a public cloud.
Provisioning architecture in which deployment of resources is performed by scripted automation and orchestration.
Provisioning virtual network appliances, such as switches, routers, and firewalls, via VMs and containers.
Services that use software-defined mechanisms and routing policies to implement virtual tunnels and overlay networks over multiple types of transport network.
An electronic system that is designed to perform a specific, dedicated function.
aka: microcontroller in a medical drip or components in a control system managing a water treatment plant.

definition: A type of OS that prioritizes deterministic execution of operations to ensure consistent response for time-critical tasks.
Network managing embedded devices
Software that aggregates and catalogs data from multiple sources within an industrial control system.
A type of industrial control system that manages large-scale, multiple-site devices and equipment spread over geographically large areas from a host computer.
Devices that can report state and configuration data and be remotely managed over IP networks.
The security design paradigm where any request (host-to-host or container-to-container) must be authenticated before being allowed.
Functions that define policy and determine access decisions.
processes that ensure each physical and data asset have an identified owner, and are appropriately tagged and classified within an inventory.

Enumeration and inventory processes and software that ensure physical and data assets comply with configuration and performance baselines, and have not been tampered with or suffered other unauthorized access.
Policies and processes that ensure asset and service purchases and contracts are fully managed, secure, use authorized suppliers/vendors, and meet business goals.
Applying consistent names and labels to assets and digital resources/ identities within a configuration management system.
A process through which an organization's information systems components are kept in a controlled state that meets the organization's requirements, including those for security and compliance.
The process through which changes to the configuration of information systems are implemented as part of the organization's overall configuration management efforts.
A security copy of production data made to removable media, typically according to a regular schedule.
Backup that writes job data to media that is stored in the same physical location as the production system.
Backup that writes job data to media that is stored in a separate physical location to the production system.
The operation to recover system functionality and/or data integrity using backup media.
Used to create the entire architectural instance/copy of an application, disk, or system.
A method used by file systems to record changes not yet made to the file system in an object called a journal.
the policies and procedures that govern the removal of devices and software from production networks, and their subsequent disposal through sale, donation, or as waste.
The process of thoroughly and completely removing data from a storage medium so that file remnants cannot be recovered.
a disposal technique that ensures that data remnants are rendered physically inaccessible and irrevocable, through degaussing, shredding, or incineration.

An asset disposal technique that relies on a third party to use sanitization or destruction methods for data remnant removal, and provides documentary evidence that the process is complete and successful.
Identifies how business processes should deal with both minor and disaster-level disruption by ensuring that there is processing redundancy supporting the workflow.
A practice which involves estimating the personnel, storage, computer hardware, software, and connection infrastructure resources required over some future period of time.
Protection against system failure by providing extra (redundant) capacity. Generally, fault tolerant systems identify and eliminate single points of failure.
An alternate processing location that is dormant or performs noncritical functions under normal conditions, but which can be rapidly converted to a key operations site if needed.
A load balancing technique where a group of servers are configured as a unit and work together to provide network services.
An advanced strip socket that provides filtered output voltage.
A battery-powered device that supplies AC power that an electronic device can use in the event of power failure.
A standby power supply fueled by diesel or propane. In the event of a power outage, a UPS must provide transitionary power, as a backup generator cannot be cut in fast enough.
Cybersecurity resilience strategy that increases attack costs by provisioning multiple types of controls, technologies, vendors, and crypto implementations.
Cybersecurity resilience tools and techniques to increase the cost of attack planning for the threat actor.
A host (honeypot), set up with the purpose of luring attackers away from assets of actual value and/or discovering attack strategies and weaknesses in the security configuration.
Deception strategy that returns spoofed data in response to network probes.
A discussion of simulated emergency situations and security incidents.
A testing technique that replicates the conditions of a real-world disaster scenario or security incident.
Running primary and backup systems simultaneously to validate the functionality and performance of backup systems without disrupting normal operations.
Physical security mechanisms that ensure a site is sufficiently illuminated for employees and guests to feel safe and for camera-based surveillance systems to work well.
Sturdy vertical post installed to control road traffic or designed to prevent ram-raiding and vehicle-ramming attacks.
A scanner that reads data from an RFID or NFC tag when in range.
Physical security control that uses cameras and recording devices to visually monitor the activity in a certain area.
A component in an alarm system that identifies unauthorized entry via infrared-, ultrasonic-, microwave-, or pressure-based detection of thermal changes or movement.
Gaining superuser-level access over an Android-based mobile device.
Removes the protective seal and any OS-specific restrictions to give users greater control over the device.
Installing an app to a mobile device without using an app store.
The potential vulnerability that occurs when there is a change between when an app checked a resource and when the app used the resource.
A program that enforces strict type-checking during compilation and ensures variables and data are used correctly. It prevents memory-related vulnerabilities and injection attacks.

A malicious script hosted on the attacker's site or coded in a link injected onto a trusted site designed to compromise clients browsing the trusted site, circumventing the browser's security model of trusted zones.
Hardware or software configured with a list of known weaknesses and exploits and that can scan for their presence in a host OS or particular application.
A scan that uses fewer permissions and many times can only find missing patches or updates.
A scan that uses credentials, such as usernames and passwords, to take a deep dive during the vulnerability scan, which will produce more information while auditing the network.
A vulnerability testing tool designed to identify issues with application code and platform configuration, including web servers and web applications.
Software testing that examines code behavior during runtime.
A list of detailed information about the software components and dependencies used in an application or system.
Tools designed to assist with identification of third-party and open-source code during software development and deployment.
Signatures and pattern-matching rules supplied to analysis platforms as an automated feed.
Blacklists of known threat sources
The science of creating machines with the ability to develop problem-solving and analysis strategies without significant human direction or intervention.
Software code or security research that remains in the ownership of the developer and may only be used under permitted license conditions.
Collaborative groups that exchange data about emerging cybersecurity threats and vulnerabilities.
A not-for-profit group set up to share sector-specific threat intelligence and security best practices among its members.
Publicly available information plus the tools used to aggregate and search it.
Analysis of historical cyberattacks and adversary actions.
Resources on the Internet that are distributed between anonymized nodes and protected from general access by multiple layers of encryption and routing.
A test that uses active tools and security utilities to evaluate security by simulating an attack on a system.
Reward scheme operated by software and web services vendors for reporting vulnerabilities.
A process that allows researchers and reviewers to safely disclose vulnerabilities to a software developer.
An audit process with a wide scope, including assessment of supply chain, configuration, support, monitoring, and cybersecurity factors.
A synchronizable list of data and scripts used to check for vulnerabilities. Also referred to as plug-ins or network vulnerability tests (NVTs).
A NIST framework that outlines various accepted practices for automating vulnerability scanning.
A scheme for identifying vulnerabilities developed by MITRE and adopted by NIST.
In security scanning, a case that is reported when it should not be.
In security scanning, a case that is not reported when it should be.
In risk calculation, the percentage of an asset's value that would be lost during a security incident or disaster scenario.
In vulnerability assessment, factors or metrics due to local network or host configuration that increase or decrease the base likelihood and impact risk level.
A strategic assessment of what level of residual risk is tolerable for an organization.
Configuration guides, benchmarks, and best practices for deploying and maintaining a network device or application server in a secure state for its given role.
A process of making a host or app configuration secure by reducing its attack surface
aka: running only necessary services, installing monitoring software to protect against malware and intrusions, and establishing a maintenance schedule to ensure the system is patched to be secure against software exploits.

definition: A device that provides a connection between wireless devices and can connect to wired networks, implementing an infrastructure mode WLAN.
Standards for authenticating and encrypting access to Wi-Fi networks.
A legacy mechanism for encrypting data sent over a wireless connection.
The mechanism used in the first version of WPA to improve the security of wireless encryption mechanisms, compared to the flawed WEP standard.
Personal authentication mechanism for Wi-Fi networks introduced with WPA3 to address vulnerabilities in the WPA-PSK method.
A high performance mode of operation for symmetric encryption. Provides a special characteristic called authenticated encryption with associated data, or AEAD.
A wireless network authentication mode where a passphrase-based mechanism is used to allow group authentication to a wireless network. The passphrase is used to derive an encryption key.
A wireless network authentication mode where the access point acts as pass-through for credentials that are verified by an AAA server.
A port-based network access control (PNAC) mechanism that allows the use of EAP authentication when a host connects to an Ethernet switch.
A general term for the collected protocols, policies, and hardware that authenticate and authorize access to a network at the device level.
A segment isolated from the rest of a private network by one or more firewalls that accepts connections from the Internet over designated ports.
A network monitoring system that uses a predefined set of rules provided by a software vendor or security personnel to identify events that are unacceptable.
A network monitoring system that detects changes in normal operating data sequences and identifies abnormal sequences.
A security monitoring tool that monitors network packets for anomalous behavior based on known signatures.
The process of detecting patterns within a dataset over time, and using those patterns to make predictions about future events or to better understand past events.
A software application or gateway that filters client requests for various types of Internet content (web, FTP, IM, and so on).
Settings for services and policy configuration for a network appliance or for a server operating in a particular application role (web server, mail server, file/print server, and so on).
Removing or severely restricting communications paths to a particular device or system.

Software capable of detecting and removing virus infections and (in most cases) other types of malware, such as worms, Trojans, rootkits, adware, spyware, password crackers, network mappers, DoS tools, and so on.
Encryption of all data on a disk (including system files, temporary files, and the pagefile).
A disk drive where the controller can automatically encrypt data that is written to it.
The private key that is used to encrypt the symmetric bulk media encryption key (MEK). This means that a user must authenticate to decrypt the MEK and access the media.
Standards for implementing device encryption on storage devices.
A small unit of supplemental code meant to address either a security problem or a functionality flaw in a software package or operating system.
Identifying, testing, and deploying OS and application updates. Patches are often classified as critical, security-critical, recommended, and optional.
A type of IDS that monitors a computer system for unexpected behavior or drastic changes to the system's state.
Endpoint protection that can detect and prevent malicious activity via signature and heuristic pattern matching.
A system that can provide automated identification of suspicious activity by user accounts and computer hosts.
Linux command for managing file permissions.
A security configuration where access is denied to any entity (software process, IP/domain, and so on) unless the entity appears on a whitelist.
A security configuration where access is generally permitted to a software process, IP/domain, or other subject unless it is listed as explicitly prohibited.
The default context-based permissions scheme provided with CentOS and Red Hat Enterprise Linux.
A software application running on a single host and designed to protect only that host.
Security framework and tools to facilitate use of personally owned devices to access corporate networks and data.
Enterprise mobile device provisioning model where the device is the property of the organization and personal use is prohibited.

Enterprise mobile device provisioning model where the device remains the property of the organization, but certain personal use, such as private email, social networking, and web browsing, is permitted.
Enterprise mobile device provisioning model where employees are offered a selection of corporate devices for work and, optionally, private use.
Process and supporting technologies for tracking, controlling, and securing the organization's mobile infrastructure.
Technology that can derive a device's location when indoors by triangulating its proximity to radio sources such as Bluetooth beacons or Wi-Fi access points.
Security control that can enforce a virtual boundary based on real-world geography.
Standards for implementing data access over cellular networks are implemented as successive generations.
aka: 2G (up to about 48 Kb/s) and 3G (up to about 42 Mb/s), there are competing GSM and CDMA provider networks. Standards for 4G (up to about 90 Mb/s) and 5G (up to about 300 Mb/s) are developed under converged LTE standards.

definition: A means of determining a receiver's position on Earth based on information received from orbital satellites.

A network scope that uses close-range wireless technologies (usually based on Bluetooth or NFC) to establish communications between personal devices, such as smartphones, laptops, and printers/peripheral devices.
Using the cellular data plan of a mobile device to provide Internet access to a laptop or PC.
Short-range, wireless radio-network-transmission medium normally used to connect two personal devices, such as a mobile phone and a wireless headset.
Sending an unsolicited message or picture message using a Bluetooth connection.
A wireless attack where an attacker gains access to unauthorized information on a device using a Bluetooth connection.
Security protocol that uses certificates for authentication and encryption to protect web communications and other application protocols.
Lists of cryptographic algorithms that a server and client can use to negotiate a secure connection.
Application protocol used for monitoring and managing network devices.
Application protocol used to transfer files between network hosts. Variants include S(ecure)FTP, FTP with SSL (FTPS and FTPES), and T(rivial)FTP.
A secure version of the File Transfer Protocol that uses a Secure Shell (SSH) tunnel as an encryption method to transfer, access, and manage files.
A type of FTP using TLS for confidentiality.
Application protocol used to send mail between hosts on the Internet.
Application protocol that enables a client to download email messages from a server mailbox to a client.
Application protocol providing a means for a client to access and manage email messages stored in a mailbox on a remote server.
A DNS record identifying hosts authorized to send mail for the domain.
A cryptographic authentication mechanism for mail utilizing a public key published as a DNS record.
Framework for ensuring proper application of SPF and DKIM, utilizing a policy published as a DNS record.
A software solution that detects and prevents sensitive information from being stored on unauthorized systems or transmitted over unauthorized networks.
Security protocol that provides authentication of DNS data and upholds DNS data integrity.
Any technique used to ensure that the data entered into a field or variable in an application is handled appropriately by that application.
The method of using a digital signature to ensure the source and integrity of source code.
A software vulnerability where an attacker is able to circumvent access controls and retrieve confidential or sensitive data from the file system or database.
An application vulnerability that is defined by how an application responds to unexpected errors that can lead to holes in the security of an app.
A mechanism to account for unexpected error conditions that might arise during code execution.
A computing environment that is isolated from a host system to guarantee that the environment runs in a controlled, secure fashion.
An event that interrupts standard operations or compromises security policy.

Procedures and guidelines covering appropriate priorities, actions, and responsibilities in the event of security incidents, divided into preparation, detection, analysis, containment, eradication/recovery, and lessons learned stages.
An incident response process that hardens systems, defines policies and procedures, establishes lines of communication, and puts resources in place.
Specific procedures that must be performed if a certain type of event is detected or reported.
An incident response process that correlates event data to determine whether they are indicators of an incident.
An incident response process in which indicators are assessed to determine validity, impact, and category.
A DoS attack mitigation strategy that directs the traffic that is flooding a target IP address to a different network for analysis.
An incident response process in which malicious tools and configurations on hosts and networks are removed.
An incident response process in which hosts, networks, and systems are brought back to a secure baseline configuration.
An analysis of events that can provide insight into how to improve response and support processes in the future.
A technique used to determine the true cause of the problem that, when removed, prevents the problem from occurring again.
A cybersecurity technique designed to detect the presence of threats that have not been discovered by normal security monitoring.
In threat hunting, using sources of threat intelligence data to automate detection of adversary IoCs and TTPs.
In threat hunting, the concept that threat actor and defender may use deception or counterattacking strategies to gain positional advantage.
